explain.say: A gentle knight was pricking on the plaine. So begins Book One of The Faerie Queene, printed in 1590. A young knight rides out with a red cross on his shield, beside a lady called Una. The panels follow his adventure.

explain.say: Look at the second panel. In a dark wood he finds Error, a half-woman, half-serpent monster who vomits books and papers. He strangles her. This is allegory: a story that is also about ideas. Here, the knight is fighting error itself. What could the books mean?

explain.say: Sort the figures. On one side, Una stands for truth and Redcrosse for holiness, and the Faerie Queene, Gloriana, honours Elizabeth the First. On the other, Duessa, false and double, who for Protestant readers also meant the Catholic Church. How does allegory let a poet talk about politics safely?

explain.say: Spenser invented his own stanza: eight lines of iambic pentameter, then a ninth, longer line of twelve syllables called an alexandrine, rhymed as on the board. That long last line makes each stanza settle like a wave. He also spelled in an old-fashioned way, to sound like Chaucer. Try reading one aloud.

faq.q: What is allegory in The Faerie Queene?
faq.a: Each book follows a knight who stands for a virtue, and the people and monsters they meet stand for ideas, sins and political or religious forces, so the story works on several levels at once.
asks: How does allegory work in Spenser?

faq.a: The lady who travels with the Redcrosse Knight in Book One. Her name means one, and she represents truth, and for Protestant readers the one true church.
Spenser's nine-line stanza: eight lines of iambic pentameter and a final alexandrine of twelve syllables, rhymed ababbcbcc. Keats, Shelley and Byron later used it.
Gloriana, the queen of Faerie Land, who never quite appears but sends out the knights. She stands for Queen Elizabeth the First, to whom the poem is dedicated.

faq.q: How is The Faerie Queene connected to Ireland?
faq.a: Spenser lived in Ireland from 1580 as a colonial official and landowner, wrote much of the poem there, and argued for harsh policies in his prose work A View of the Present State of Ireland.

facts: Books I to III of The Faerie Queene appeared in 1590, and Books IV to VI in 1596.
Spenser planned twelve books but completed only six.
Spenser was buried in Westminster Abbey near Chaucer in 1599.
